analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income tax rates with a flat 17% tax and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsor flat tax bill with zero cosponsors died quietly in committee in the 114th Congress, never receiving a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The SMART Act would scrap the entire income tax code and replace it with a single 17% tax on wages, retirement income, and unemployment benefits, plus a 17% tax on business profits. It repeals the estate tax, the gift tax, the alternative minimum tax, and every income tax credit, including the earned income tax credit and child tax credit. It would also slap a 17% tax on employer-provided benefits like health insurance, and repeal rules that require pension plans to cover lower-paid workers. Finally, it would require a three-fifths vote of both chambers to pass any future bill that raises a tax rate or reduces the standard deduction.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners and owners of wealth gain the most: the top income tax rate drops sharply to 17%, the estate and gift taxes on large inheritances disappear entirely, and the alternative minimum tax is repealed. Businesses gain a lower flat profit tax and, if they sponsor a pension plan with a surplus, can pull those excess assets out without the current penalty tax. Employers and pension sponsors also gain because rules requiring plans to cover and benefit lower-paid workers are repealed, and limits on how much can be contributed are removed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and pension sponsors

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated income tax, whose top rate was 39.6% at the time, with a single 17% rate on taxable income, the largest percentage cuts going to the highest earners.
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely for deaths and gifts after 2015, eliminating federal tax on the largest inheritances.
Repeals the alternative minimum tax, which chiefly falls on high-income taxpayers with large deductions.
Repeals limits on pension contributions and restrictions on distributions, allowing far larger tax-advantaged retirement accounts for high earners.

Allows employers to transfer excess pension plan assets back to themselves and count them as income, repealing the current tax on such reversions and permitting transfers without terminating the plan.
Repeals pension nondiscrimination, minimum participation, and coverage rules, freeing plan sponsors from requirements that protected lower-paid workers.

analysis.who_pays: Working families pay through the loss of every income tax credit, including the earned income tax credit and the child tax credit, which are the main tax benefits for low- and middle-income households. Workers would effectively pay a new 17% tax on employer-provided benefits such as health insurance, since the tax falls on the employer and employers would likely scale back or drop those benefits. Some employers, particularly tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local governments, owe a new 17% tax on the noncash benefits they provide. The bill also makes future tax increases much harder, requiring a three-fifths vote of both chambers to raise a rate, lower the standard deduction, or pass anything that reduces federal revenues.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working families losing credits and benefits

drawbacks.text: Repeals all income tax credits, wiping out the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, and education credits that reduce or eliminate tax bills for millions of working households.

Imposes a 17% tax on employer-paid benefits other than cash wages and retirement contributions, which would make employer-provided health insurance far more expensive and give employers a strong reason to cut it.
Cuts the top individual rate from 39.6% to 17% and eliminates the estate tax with no offsetting revenue provision in the bill, implying very large revenue losses.
Repeals pension nondiscrimination and minimum coverage rules, removing the protections that prevent retirement plans from being designed almost entirely for executives and higher-paid employees.

Locks in the new system by declaring it out of order to consider any bill that raises a tax rate, reduces the standard deduction, or reduces federal revenues, waivable only by a three-fifths vote of both chambers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers its largest gains at the top: high earners get a big rate cut, the wealthiest families get inheritance taxes eliminated, and plan sponsors get freer hands with pension surpluses. The costs fall on ordinary households, who would lose the tax credits that matter most to them, face an effective tax on employer health coverage, and lose pension protections. For a reader without large income from wealth or a large expected inheritance, this bill was a net loss. Its simplification appeal, a single rate and no alternative minimum tax, is real but comes bundled with a permanent supermajority lock that would make it nearly impossible to later raise rates on high earners even if circumstances changed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the 114th Congress; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and the Congress ended with it dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Rogers (R-AL) introduced the bill on April 15, 2015, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in part, the House Rules Committee.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its lifetime.
No further action was ever recorded: Ways and Means never scheduled a markup and the bill never reached the House floor.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the bill receiving any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, working families kept the earned income tax credit, the child tax credit, and the current treatment of employer health insurance, and high earners, large estates, and pension sponsors did not get the rate cuts, estate tax repeal, and pension rule rollback they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working families who kept their tax credits

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll-call evidence exists; the only recorded support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill cuts the top individual rate to 17%, repeals the alternative minimum tax, and abolishes the estate and gift taxes entirely. Its largest dollar benefits flow to high earners and families inheriting large estates, while the credits ordinary households rely on are repealed.

Business profits are taxed at a flat 17%, replacing the up-to-35% corporate rate, a substantial cut. But employers also owe a new 17% tax on noncash employee benefits like health insurance, and the practical burden would likely reach workers through reduced benefits.

The bill repeals contribution limits, distribution restrictions, and nondiscrimination rules, and lets employers withdraw excess pension assets without the penalty tax, with only normal income inclusion. These changes free plan sponsors at the expense of protections for lower-paid plan participants.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local governments
industries.note: These employers would owe a new 17% tax on noncash benefits they provide to employees, a cost currently not imposed, which would likely be passed to workers or taxpayers.

Higher standard deductions shield some income, but the loss of all credits, the flat rate that replaces progressive brackets, and taxation of employer benefits leave most working households paying more than they would under current law.
